issues.problem: The signature product is a duck-canvas chore coat with a corduroy collar in duck brown. That is nearly item for item the Carhartt Detroit Jacket, from a Dearborn company Detroit treats as its own. The brief says "never echo Carhartt marks" but gives no way to avoid competing with the hero garment on its home turf. A Pistons logo on a Carhartt silhouette reads as imitation. The duck brown and safety yellow palette also sits outside the Pistons' royal, red and navy, which invites NBA and Pistons brand-approval friction.
issues.fix: Pick one. Approach Carhartt (Dearborn) for a licensed, credited collaboration. Or move away from its codes: knit, fleece and technical shell constructions, a Pistons-blue field with a plant-floor stencil, and brown or yellow only as small hits. Clear the palette with the Pistons and NBA before it anchors a collection.

issues.problem: "Unfinished business" and "run it back" fail the swap test. Cleveland, Boston or any team that lost a second-round Game 7 could use them. "April revenge pack" assumes a Cleveland rematch that may never happen. The 125-94 margin is also still raw, so selling it back to fans can feel like salt in the wound. What is Detroit-specific is the work-first, counted-out voice (Goin' to Work, the Detroit vs. Everybody stance), not the loss.
issues.fix: Write the campaign in Detroit labor language: shift, clock-in, overtime, punch card, built to be worn in. Keep "unfinished business" as quiet subtext, not a graphic. Rename the April pack for work or the playoffs, not Cleveland, and keep Cleveland-specific copy out of the pre-built line.

issues.problem: The brief treats opening night as the "Specter launch". It adds a "Specter-companion" hoodie and a Specter collector capsule sold "on wear dates only". The verified facts say Specter was revealed on Sep 9, with its merchandise released the same day. The wear games haven't been captured. So the brief launches something already on shelves and promises wear-date-only availability for product already sold. That misreads the calendar and Nike's own release.
issues.fix: Reframe Oct 20 as the first Detroit moment after the Sep 9 reveal, built around the confirmed national game rather than a launch claim. Replace the wear-date-only capsule with in-arena stories and sell-in support. Confirm wear dates before tying any product to one.

issues.problem: Uniform designs for 2026-27 are locked and in production, and Detroit's 2026-27 City Edition is unverified. Glaze can only be a 2027-28 concept, and a City Edition slot isn't Nike's to give: the NBA and the Pistons approve every set. Yet the calendar sells Glaze satin bombers, motto crewnecks and a Glaze shoe from Black Friday through March. That spends Pewabic's story on lifestyle product a year before any uniform exists.
issues.fix: Present the uniform as a 2027-28 pitch to the NBA and Pistons, with a lead-time plan. This season, run only a small test-and-learn Pewabic lifestyle story. Hold the shoe and hero pieces until the uniform is approved.

issues.problem: Calling Pewabic teal "a Detroit color nobody else owns" overreaches. Pewabic is known for iridescent glazes across greens, blues and golds. The link to the 1990s Pistons teal is Nike's own designer logic, and the dossiers show no fan making it. It also risks pleasing no one: teal-era fans may read it as a back-door reissue, and design-literate locals as co-opted craft.
issues.fix: Test it with named Detroit fans and Pewabic before it carries the uniform. Lead with the real stories: the glaze process, and the tile in Detroit buildings and People Mover stations. Use teal as one accent, not the base, until the fan link is proven.

issues.problem: The bomber is named for Livernois' Avenue of Fashion, a Black-owned dress-culture corridor. No Livernois designer, tailor or boutique is named in the partners list or credited on the product.
issues.fix: Name and pay a Livernois-based designer or shop as co-designer, credit them on the tag, and put the first release in their door. Otherwise drop the Avenue of Fashion name.

issues.problem: The techno capsule is the highest-risk lane. Underground Resistance has a long anti-corporate stance, and the brief's palette (black, signal red), photocopy-flyer prints and anonymous-collective look are close to UR's own visual language, even without its marks. The KPI "renew for 2028" assumes a partner who may decline. Movement has its own promoter, so Nike can't simply "own" the weekend. The Memorial Day overlap with a conference-finals run is speculative.
issues.fix: Make the lane contingent. First test a few Detroit techno artists and labels, including newer ones, and proceed only with a written, paid, co-owned agreement. Plan a no-go branch. Drop the red-and-black flyer look if UR isn't involved. Treat the arena walk-in track as the lower-risk, higher-value piece.

issues.problem: Naming Tee Grizzley and Sada Baby as opening-night ambassadors commits Nike to people before any vetting. The music dossier flags Detroit rap's Eastside and Westside rivalries and street-content baggage. The brief doesn't say how a pairing would be chosen or what happens if it goes wrong.
issues.fix: Name a vetted shortlist instead of individuals, and include non-rap Detroit voices (a producer, a chef, a PSL alum). Choose on fit, conduct and local standing, with a clear approval step.

issues.problem: Detroit vs. Everybody is the only collaborator named for the biggest city-first opportunity, and "status to confirm" keeps recurring. Black History Month is also the only point where Black Detroit creators get a dedicated drop, which can read as a seasonal gesture rather than a commitment. With one brand carrying the pillar, a no from DVE collapses it.
issues.fix: Name two or three alternates now (other Black-owned Detroit labels, shops and designers). Run the collab as a rolling roster across the season with a standing revenue share, not a single February drop.

issues.problem: Three Eras launches on MLK Day, an away game at noon in Cleveland, with watch parties tied to a revenge angle. Launching a retail line on that holiday sits badly with the brief's own "respectful" note. The line's sales window (Feb-March) is also a month later. And the watch-party venues are shaky: Hockeytown Cafe is a Red Wings bar, and its operating status is unverified.
issues.fix: Use MLK Day for community and civic giving, not a product launch. Move the Three Eras launch to early February, ahead of the deadline and the profit-sharing window. Hold watch parties at Checker Bar or another Pistons-neutral Detroit venue.

issues.problem: The pack leads with Duren and Ausar Thompson "rather than star worship," but the retail-behavior dossier says Cade dominates jersey demand. He is the All-NBA First Team face of the franchise. The bandwagon fan buys the star, and that fan is the pack's own customer. The Spirit of Detroit jersey moment also depends on the city and on a protected work, and the culture dossier says to check rights.
issues.fix: Lead the playoff jersey line with Cade and use effort graphics for the rest. Treat the Spirit of Detroit moment as the city's own tradition, with any product use cleared with the city. It is not a Nike event.

issues.problem: Ramadan 2027 should fall roughly Feb 8 to Mar 9. Eid al-Fitr falls around Mar 9-10. Both land across the brief's Feb-March premium push. Dearborn, Hamtramck and Southwest Detroit have core Pistons fans. Yet the brief mentions Arab American and Bangladeshi communities only as a risk, with no partner, product or timing for them. Pączki Day (Feb 9) is the only community moment it uses, and it has a weak product link.
issues.fix: Check game tip times against iftar, since late-day starts matter. Plan an Eid gifting and family-sizing push for Fairlane and Dearborn, with named Arab American and Bangladeshi Detroit creators as paid partners, and verify moon-sighting dates. Cut the Pączki speckle tee or make it a community donation only.

issues.problem: The underground dossier's jit and ghettotech idea is one of the few Detroit-only footwear and apparel briefs (traction, ankle freedom, low-profile court shoes with dancers). The brief reduces it to nothing. The only shoe it proposes is a Pewabic "Glaze" colorway, which is a color story, not a product insight.
issues.fix: Add a credited, paid test program with Detroit jit dancers, choreographers and PSL players for traction and fit. Make that, not a colorway, the footwear story.

issues.problem: The food dossier's strongest local argument, Lafayette vs. American Coney, gets no launch idea. Neither does the pan-pizza and Little Caesars Arena naming link. The brief is also silent on Detroit Shock heritage and the Motor City Cruise. And it ignores the departure of Isaiah Stewart, the longest-tenured Piston and a natural grit symbol.
issues.fix: Add a light, licensed Coney "pick a side" graphic idea, or leave it out deliberately. Add a heritage women's line. Plan a clear-out for Stewart jerseys, with a respectful send-off rather than a feature.

issues.problem: Cup-night limited tees at LCA and a Hinkle Fieldhouse road-trip pack are padding. Cup merchandise belongs to the NBA's Cup program, not to a Nike Detroit plan. The knockout contingency also depends on seeding that can't be planned.
issues.fix: Cut the road-trip pack. Keep only an unbranded Cup contingency with pre-approved blanks, which costs nothing if Detroit isn't a higher seed.

issues.problem: The Feb-March premium push assumes Detroit Three profit-sharing and tax refunds. Payout size and timing are unverified for the 2026 cycle and tied to no named source. Four of seven opportunities are priority 1, which dilutes the plan, and the rhythm dossier advises saving the peak for April.
issues.fix: Confirm 2026 payout news before building the push on it. Cap priority 1 at opening night, the winter outerwear program and the April pack, and move the rest to priority 2.

issues.problem: Culture 93 against retail 58 is defensible. But "among the league's deepest" compares across markets, which this single-market brief can't support. The retail score also rests on unverified partner doors (DVE, Burn Rubber, Inner State, Nike Factory at Great Lakes Crossing).
issues.fix: Qualify the cultural score as a judgment. Lower the confidence on the retail score until the doors are confirmed.

strengths: Detroit-first, city-before-crest is the right insight. It is well evidenced across lenses, and it relies on named, paid, credited makers rather than imitation.
Workwear as sportswear and a seven-month coat-and-hoodie season give the assortment a real local reason to exist. The price ladder is sensible, with a suburban volume split.
Three era lanes (Bad Boys, teal, Cade) respect a genuine generation gap and keep the eras apart.
The brief steers clear of ruin imagery, "comeback city" language and Rust Belt cliches. It also flags IP and licensing for Motown, Carhartt, UR and the city seal.
The calendar respects the Lions' Thanksgiving, the missing Christmas Day game, the Oct 20 national tipoff and the April peak.
summary: A strong, locally grounded brief. Its core (Detroit-first, workwear, paid local co-authors) holds up, but four things need fixing. The Shift Change coat is too close to Carhartt's own Detroit Jacket. "Unfinished business" is a generic sports line. The Specter launch framing ignores the Sep 9 release. The Glaze uniform is a 2027-28 pitch, not a 2026-27 product. The techno lane is the riskiest partnership. The biggest missed openings are Arab American and Bangladeshi Detroit, jit dance, and Ramadan and Eid timing.
